[TITLE: "The Price of a Name"]
[SYNOPSIS: In the Veilwood clearing, Lirael’s first supervision of a First Sacrifice shatters when the youth redirects her offering toward Lirael’s buried past. The misalignment draws every eye, including Julian’s silent watch at the edge, and the rite’s public failure now threatens both her qualification and the fragile distance she keeps from the one man who already sees too much.]

The youth’s voice rose clear through the mated-pair veil. “I give the discipline to finish my studies and train as a Sacrificiant.”

I felt the alignment settle, true and clean, the way it should on a First Sacrifice. Then her eyes found mine.

“I give it instead so she finds the father who left her.”

The words landed wrong. The sacrifice she had prepared belonged to one desire; the wish now belonged to another. Everyone present felt the sour note at once. Trained or not, the misalignment rang through the clearing like a struck flaw in glass.

Julian stood perfectly still at the outer ring, slate-blue skin catching the dawn light that filtered through the canopy. His long black hair curtained the side of his face as he lowered his head a fraction, the small silver scar at his left wrist the only movement I could see. I remembered the way those fingers once moved across wet clay, precise and unhurried, as if the shape already existed and he was only agreeing to free it. The memory pulled heat up my throat before I could stop it.

The presiding Dohkar’s hands lifted, too late. The bargain had already been offered and the price had already been claimed by the wrong shape.

I tore the gossamer band from my mouth. The cloth whispered against my skin as it fell. Protocol broke with it. Every First Favored turned.

Julian’s gaze lifted. He did not speak. The Weave-Script on his forearms moved in slow harmonic loops, a private language I had no right to read. I wanted to know what he saw when he looked at me now—whether the youth’s wish had confirmed the rumor or simply given him another test I had not chosen to take.

The assembly’s silence pressed closer. Someone would speak soon. Someone would ask why the Sacrificiant had moved at all.

My hand tightened around my great-grandmother’s old tarot deck. I didn't remember bringing it. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.

before:
The youth’s voice rose clear through the mated-pair veil. “I give the discipline to finish my studies and train as a Sacrificiant.” The words twisted mid-air as the youth pivoted on the stone, eyes locking on mine while the clearing’s air thickened and the First Favored nearest the circle jerked their heads toward the Dohkar. I shoved forward through the seated ring, knees scraping the ritual mat, and seized the youth’s wrist before the Dohkar’s hands could rise to seal the offering. 

The misalignment hit like a live current up my arms. My pulse slammed against the mated-pair veil still clinging to my mouth, and the youth’s skin burned hot under my grip as she tried to wrench free. Every head in the assembly snapped toward us. The Dohkar’s voice cracked across the space, demanding the rite resume, but the youth’s altered wish had already pulled the Weave taut in the wrong direction and the clearing itself seemed to lean inward, waiting for the fracture to split wider. 

Julian’s name cut through the rising murmurs from the outer ring, spoken by someone at his shoulder, and his slate-blue form shifted one step closer to the light. I kept my hold on the youth and forced the words out anyway, naming the original sacrifice aloud so the Dohkar could not pretend the bargain remained intact. The youth’s free hand clawed at the air as if to snatch the words back, but the Weave-Script along Julian’s forearms flared once in answer, drawing every eye to the place where his gaze met mine across the circle. 

I dragged the youth two paces toward the central stone, refusing to release her until the Dohkar acknowledged the break. The assembly’s silence fractured into overlapping questions—why the wish had changed, whether the father she named even lived, what price the veil would now demand. My fingers tightened around the youth’s wrist until she stopped struggling, and I turned my shoulder to block Julian’s line of sight while the Dohkar’s staff struck the ground once, twice, ordering the rite to continue under the new terms. The pressure in my chest sharpened into a single demand: either claim the altered sacrifice as my own or let the misalignment brand every Favored present. I stepped between the youth and the Dohkar, voice steady, and named the correction that would force the Weave back into alignment before the dawn light shifted again.
